title: Mild hypothermia (cold exposure, person still alert)
summary: Shivering, cold pale skin, slow thinking, clumsy hands after long cold exposure. Catching it early is straightforward — getting it wrong (rough handling, hot water, alcohol) is dangerous.
steps: Move the person out of the wind and cold to a sheltered, warm place.
Replace any wet clothes with dry warm ones. If you have no dry clothes, wrap them — wet clothes and all — in a blanket or sleeping bag along with another warm person.
Insulate them from the ground with a mat, blanket, or jackets. Cold ground pulls heat out faster than cold air.
Cover the head, neck, and torso first. Most heat is lost from these areas.
If they can swallow safely and are fully alert, give warm sweet drinks — not alcohol, not coffee.
Encourage gentle movement once they have started to warm up — large muscle activity speeds rewarming.
Watch them closely for the next hour. Shivering should ease as they warm; if it gets worse or they get sleepy or confused, get medical help.
avoid: Do not rub or massage the limbs vigorously — cold blood from the limbs returning to the heart can trigger dangerous heart rhythms.
Do not put the person in a hot bath or shower, or against a hot fire or stove.
Do not give alcohol, coffee, or sedatives.
Do not assume they are safe once they stop shivering — this can also be a sign of worsening hypothermia.
whenToEscalate: Emergency immediately if: shivering stops while still cold, speech becomes slurred, they become drowsy, confused, or unconscious, or their pulse slows.
Anyone pulled from cold water, an avalanche, or trapped outdoors overnight — emergency.
Infants, elderly, and anyone with diabetes or thyroid disease — see a doctor even after apparent recovery.
Frostbite of fingers, toes, ears, nose, or face along with hypothermia — see [[frostbite-early]] and seek medical care.
specialty: Emergency department; high-altitude clinic in Ladakh-type regions.
